items.title: The Landing, Beloved Los Angeles Gallery with a Keen Eye for Pairing Historical and Contemporary Artists, Closes After 14 Years
items.summary:
The Landing, a beloved Los Angeles gallery whose program was defined by its unique pairings of historical and contemporary artists, announced that it had closed. Its last exhibition was a one-night only solo for Maxwell Hendler staged on October 29.

On the gallery’s website, founder and owner Gerard O’Brien wrote, “the Landing Gallery at 5118 W Jefferson Blvd is now closed. We are no longer programming at this location. We are deeply grateful to the artists, collectors, collaborators, and community who have been fellow participants in our engagements. It has been a privilege to champion extraordinary artists, present ambitious exhibitions, and create a space for meaningful exchange and discovery.”

In an Instagram post , Gerard O’Brien put it more simply, “End of an era … 22 years of Gallery spaces in Los Angeles, Reform Galley 2004-2019 … the Landing Gallery 2012 -2026 … onwards. thank you Los Angeles❣️”

O’Brien founded the Landing in 2012 as an off-shoot of his design-focused Reform Gallery. “I never really thought there was a big difference,” he said of the distinction between art and design. He chose the name for its original location, a spot within Reform: “he cleared out the landing atop a short staircase in his furniture gallery and dedicated it to shows of art, bringing in work by artists both contemporary and historical to display just above his design wares,” as a 2016 blog post by book publisher Phaidon reported .

In 2015, O’Brien decided that it was time for the Landing to grow, opening in a 2,800-square-foot gallery space on Jefferson Boulevard with a solo…
items.t: The Landing, Beloved Los Angeles Gallery with a Keen Eye for Pairing Historical and Contemporary Artists, Closes After 14 Years

items.title: Drawing Center's Laura Hoptman Wins Curatorial Excellence Award
items.summary:
Art Movements,  published every Thursday afternoon, is a roundup of must-know news, appointments, awards, and other happenings in today’s chaotic art world. 

Laura Hoptman Wins CCS Bard Audrey Irmas Award for Curatorial Excellence The Center for Curatorial Studies at Bard College announced Laura Hoptman , executive director of the Drawing Center in New York, as the recipient of the 2027 Audrey Irmas Award for Curatorial Excellence, a $25,000 prize. Hoptman's curriculum vitae reads like a roll call of NYC's major institutions: She started out as an assistant curator at the Bronx Museum in the 1980s and later held curatorial roles at the Museum of Modern Art and the New Museum. 

So it is no surprise that, when asked what this recognition signified for her, Hoptman chose to invoke the network and community that her career has grown alongside.

“The best kind of professional recognition comes from one's peers, and this is one of the many reasons why this award is so meaningful to me,” Hoptman told Hyperallergic in an email. “It also reminds me how damn lucky I have been to have spent the last 30 years around art and artists in one of the greatest cultural hubs in the world. After all this time, my vocation still fills me with joy.”
items.t: Drawing Center's Laura Hoptman Wins Curatorial Excellence Award

items.title: Frieze Abu Dhabi Debuts to Brisk Sales and Confident Dealers
items.summary:
On the morning of Frieze Abu Dhabi’s inaugural edition, Saudi Arabia’s financial center in Riyadh was reportedly attacked by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels. The crowd in Abu Dhabi, at least, had other things on their minds: the fair was about to open, with millions of dollars’ worth of art ready to be sold. Members of the royal family were back after getting a sneak peek yesterday, alongside politicians and celebrities including tennis star Venus Williams and architect Kulapat Yantrasast.

“It’s about time. Frieze is bringing its A-game to Abu Dhabi, where they have the best museums,” Yantrasast told ARTnews , cheekily mentioning that he’s been putting dots on artworks from The Third Line, Taymour Grahne Projects, Experimenter and Pearl Lam Projects. 

The dealers were in high spirits too, as booths started to get busy an hour after the opening. At Thaddeus Ropac, three of Imran Qureshi’s Water Bodies sold for $60,000, each to a UAE-based collection, though the gallery declined to specify whether this was a private or institutional collection.

“There is a great energy around the fair in Abu Dhabi this week. We’re having good conversations with collectors who are well-informed about the artists we are presenting, and you can feel the impact of the institutional scene here,” Xenia Geroulanos, director at Thaddaeus Ropac, told ARTnews .

Venus Williams at ArtAncient’s booth at Frieze Abu Dhabi 2026.

items.title: Ahmed Morsi, Whose Poetic Paintings Long for His Egyptian Homeland, Dies at 96
items.summary:
Ahmed Morsi, an Egyptian-born, New York–based painter and poet who once said he had been “displaced most of my life,” died on Wednesday at the age of 96. His death by natural causes in Cairo was confirmed his daughter Sherine Morsi. 

In an Instagram post announcing the artist’s death, Sherine wrote, “His profound understanding of our shared humanity, in all its complexity, fragility, and beauty, found expression in both his art and his words.”

Born in Alexandria, Egypt, in 1930, Ahmed Morsi studied drawing in his early years with the Italian artist Silvio Bicchi and became part of the so-called Alexandria School devoted to Surrealist imagery around the time of World War II. But, as he told ARTnews ’s Alex Greenberger in 2021, “We need to distinguish between the geographic place that is Egypt’s second largest city from my ‘home.’ My Alexandria is a city of my youth and also myth and legend. This is the ‘home’ that has fueled my imagination, spilling into my poetry notebooks and pouring over my canvas. Don’t look for this Alexandria on your maps.”

After developing his distinctive painting style—poetic figuration with a quiet sense of fantasy suffused with muted hues—in Egypt and Iraq in the 1950s and ’60s, Morsi moved to New York in 1974 when his wife, Amany Fahmy, got a job as chief of the United Nations Arabic Translation Service. She helped translate some of Morsi’s writing, which took different forms ranging from poetry to art criticism, including the founding of Galerie 68 , an influential journal devoted to Arabic modernism based in Cairo. 

About his writing, which…
items.t: Ahmed Morsi, Whose Poetic Paintings Long for His Egyptian Homeland, Dies at 96

items.title: Rare Hilma af Klint Painting Sells for Staggering $12.7M
items.summary:
Hilma af Klint's painting “Ser III No. 5” (1920) sold for a record $12.7 million (SEK 128.9 million) at Bukowskis's modern art and design auction in Stockholm today, November 19, fetching over 16 times the upper end of its estimated price. 

The first abstract painting by the Swedish artist and "mother of abstraction" to appear on the open market in 30 years, "Ser III No. 5" was one of the 85 geometric paintings the artist produced during a fervent months-long process in 1920. Theosophical symbols, triangles, and circles in "Ser III No. 5" provide insight into af Klint's last engagement with geometric abstraction before she turned to more naturalist watercolors in the last years of her life.
items.t: Rare Hilma af Klint Painting Sells for Staggering $12.7M

items.title: Benin Puts Pressure on Musée du Quai Branly in Paris to Return 35 Looted Objects
items.summary:
A lot has happened between November 2021, when France formally returned 26 Benin Bronzes from its national collections to Benin, and today, when news of the West African nation’s latest request was reported by Le Monde . Namely, in May 2026, French Parliament passed a historic law designed to simplify the process by which artworks looted during the colonial era are returned to their nations of origin.

The latest request was first broached last summer and reiterated in the fall, when Beninese President Romuald Wadagni visited Paris and met with French President Emmanuel Macron. Like the 2021 repatriation, the new request is directed to the Musée du Quai Branly – Jacques Chirac, whose collection is made up of objects from Indigenous groups in Africa, Asia, and Oceania.

“We felt somewhat unsatisfied after the first return,” Alain Godonou, project manager for heritage and museums for the presidency of Benin, told Le Monde . “We drew up a second list which, in our view, meets the criteria for return under the [new] law. We are confident in our rightful claim.”

The latest request includes a divination tray and several types of weapons. But the most important object still in the French state’s collection is a hammered iron sculpture of Gou, a god of metalworking and war. This particular representation of Gou was made by Akati Ekplekendo in the mid-19th century and was taken from Benin by the French captain Eugène Fonssagrives in 1892. The 5½-foot-tall sculpture was one of 600 objects included in the 1935 exhibition “African Negro Art” at the Museum of Modern Art in New York…
items.t: Benin Puts Pressure on Musée du Quai Branly in Paris to Return 35 Looted Objects

items.title: The Ebullient Ecofeminism of Carolina Caycedo
items.summary:
ST LOUIS, MO — A pink lake under an avalanche of digital detritus; a neon rainbow behind a man in a hazmat suit; a gilt sky above a lone wind turbine. These are among the surreal, meticulously rendered scenes in Carolina Caycedo’s series Mineral Intensive (2023–ongoing). 

Caycedo’s candy-colored drawings lure the eye only to disquiet the mind, exposing the contradictions of so-called clean energy, whose production often depends on environmentally destructive mineral extraction.

Such visual beguilement — and ecological exigency — anchors Carolina Caycedo: Growing Deep Roots , an exhibition of sculpture, video, printmaking, and drawing that explores the joyous, multisensory dimensions of the artist’s activism.

Born and raised in Bogotá, Colombia, the Los Angeles-based artist devoted two years to collaborative research with botanists, plant taxonomists, and Native elders, informing her rendering of prairie and botanical life across the Mississippi River watershed. By turns bright and delicate, Caycedo’s Plant Portraits series (2021–ongoing) lends an ecofeminist bent to the larger show, merging feminine anatomy with botanical illustration.

Like a heavenly necklace, “Celestial Autonomy, the Dance of Big Dipper and North Star” (2023) dangles in the center of the gallery. Constructed of Alaskan…
items.t: The Ebullient Ecofeminism of Carolina Caycedo

items.title: Laia Abril Photographs the Instruments of Rape Culture
items.summary:
Editor’s Note: The following story contains mentions of sexual assault and harassment. To reach the National Sexual Assault Hotline, call 1-800-656-HOPE (4673) or visit  online.rainn.org . 

Some institutional rape cases create a glut of content. Recent allegations against Cornell students led to the publication of the accused’s portraits, images of their text messages, and videos of their fraternity house. Tweets and articles flooded the internet, while a journalist’s attempt to identify Jane Doe launched an entire Instagram campaign : Users posted their own pictures with the hashtag #iamjanedoe to help shield the victim. On the other side of the spectrum, reported rapes in the military, the Catholic Church, and less wealthy communities around the world may be met with silence, handled privately, or otherwise fail to galvanize the digital realm. 

Spanish photographer Laia Abril — whose larger project “A History of Misogyny” has also tackled feminicide, abortion, and endometriosis — faces a tricky mandate as she created On Rape and Institutional Failure , first shown in 2020 and now on view at the International Center for Photography. Her images have to be compelling without embracing spectacle, specific while addressing an enormous, global theme. 

The artist makes two key choices, one conceptual and one formal: She shoots objects instead of people, all in black-and-white. Honing in on her palette, Abril gets at the seemingly eternal nature of misogyny; her distilled images stoke a similarly condensed rage.
items.t: Laia Abril Photographs the Instruments of Rape Culture

items.title: Art Dealer Sentenced for Falsely Claiming Native Heritage
items.summary:
This month, a Las Vegas man pled guilty to a felony violation of the Indian Arts and Crafts Act of 1990 after being charged with selling counterfeit Native American art misrepresented as authentic to consumers. A United States district court judge for Nevada sentenced Jose Martinez, who adopted the name Joseph Skywolf, to two years of supervised probation and court-ordered restitution for the infraction. 

A release from the US Department of the Interior's Indian Arts and Crafts Board (IACB) outlined that Martinez falsely claimed to be Chiricahua Apache, Apache, Navajo, and Native American while promoting his mobile business Skywolf's Gallery. Through the business, which was once headquartered in Jackson, Wyoming, but traveled to venues and markets across the Great Plains and Southwest, Martinez deliberately sold counterfeit artwork and handicrafts, including headdresses, jewelry, paintings, and beaded tanned hides falsely attributed to Native artists or specific tribes. 

Last summer, Martinez was indicted on one count of violating the Indian Arts and Crafts Act, which prohibits the sale of products falsely marketed as authentic American Indian or Alaska Native art and craftwork. The act is intended to protect the livelihoods, cultural knowledge, and artistic traditions of recognized Native tribes, bands, and communities, as well as consumers seeking authentic cultural heritage and art objects.
items.t: Art Dealer Sentenced for Falsely Claiming Native Heritage

items.title: Piaget’s Latest Release Is a Limited-Edition Andy Warhol Camouflage Watch
items.summary:
Where do the worlds of art and watchmaking intersect? One place is the Andy Warhol Watch line, which the luxury Swiss watch brand Piaget has released since 2024 in collaboration with the Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts.

To learn more about Piaget’s history with Warhol and its ongoing partnership with the Warhol Foundation, Jean-Bernard Forot, Piaget’s Head of Patrimony, joined ARTnews for a conversation as part of the inaugural Art Week NYC , a citywide festival celebrating contemporary art.

Forot spoke about the history of the Maison Piaget, which was founded in 1874 in the idyllic village of La Côte-aux-Fées (a translation of which is “fairy hills”), as well as the company’s two manufactures , in La Côte-aux-Fées and Geneva, where the watches are conceived and produced. Having those two locations, he said, “creates a tension and creates a creativity that is really interesting.”

In the postwar era, Piaget became known for its bold designs featuring precious gold and ornamental stones. When it opened a US flagship on Fifth Avenue, it attracted high-profile clients like Elizabeth Taylor, Elvis Presley, and Jackie Kennedy—all of whom were subjects of Warhol’s art.

Warhol soon became a client of Piaget’s and befriended Yves Piaget, the company’s longtime chairman. The Pop artist came to own at least seven Piagets, including the cushion-shaped Black Tie Watch, which Forot speculated captured Warhol’s attention for its resemblance to a TV screen. After the company reissued it decades later, collectors lovingly called it the Warhol Watch, which ultimately led…
items.t: Piaget’s Latest Release Is a Limited-Edition Andy Warhol Camouflage Watch

items.title: Native Artist Receives $10K Grant to Revive Visor Craftmaking
items.summary:
The Walker Youngbird Foundation named Native artist Dustin Newman (Unangax̂/Deg Hit’an Athabascan) the annual recipient of its Núhi grant today, November 19. The Alaskan artist will use the $10,000 award to revive and pass down the endangered craftsmanship behind qayaatx̂ux , traditional closed crown visors worn by Unangax̂ chiefs. 

Through technical research with the Anchorage Museum and collaborations with regional hat-makers, Newman will produce a small series of visors to gift to cultural leaders. An intricately decorated hunting hat historically worn by chiefs and high-ranking whaling captains, the qayaatx̂ux began fading into obscurity in the early 20th century due to factors including American colonization. After completing the series, Newman will share the tradition with community members through Camp Qungaayux on the island of Unalaska and the Agdaagux Culture Camp in King Cove, the fishing village where the artist was raised. 

"I first started bending visors at 17 with my mentor Okalena Patricia Lekanoff-Gregory at our regional culture camp in Anchorage and Unalaska," Newman told Hyperallergic . "Why I chose to pursue this project through the Núhi Grant was to uplift the status of these visors not as a wall hanging but as a symbol within our communities honoring our culture bearers and community leaders."
items.t: Native Artist Receives $10K Grant to Revive Visor Craftmaking

items.title: Amsterdam’s Stedelijk Museum Names Krist Gruijthuijsen as Next Director
items.summary:
The Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam has named the Dutch-born curator and art critic Krist Gruijthuijsen as its next director. He will succeed Rein Wolfs in July 2027.

Gruijthuijsen, a self-described “artist-driven curator,” will join the Stedelijk from EMMA – Espoo Museum of Modern Art in Finland, where he has been director since 2025, a role he holds concurrently with curator at large at Kunsthaus Zürich.

His vision for EMMA, a respected but relatively low-profile institution outside the Nordic region, included sustained support for artists through project funding, acquisitions and stipends, among more. Speaking to Frieze , he said he envisioned opening up the floor of the Brutalist building by removing its internal walls. 

Prior to EMMA, Gruijthuijsen was director of the KW Institute for Contemporary Art in Berlin, beginning in 2016. His tenure there included well-received programming, with exhibitions by artists such as Hanne Lippard, Beatriz González, and Hassan Sharif. He also curated “Martin Wong: Malicious Mischief,” which the Stedelijk co-produced and hosted from November 2023 to April 2024.

His return to Amsterdam will also mark a curatorial homecoming, as Gruijthuijsen cofounded the Kunstverein Amsterdam with Maxine Kopsa and served as its director from 2009 to 2012, a role that briefly overlapped with his time heading the MA Fine Arts department at Amsterdam’s Sandberg Instituut (2011-16). 

At the Stedelijk, he will oversee the institution’s modern and contemporary art and design strategy and guide collection management and public engagement.

items.title: Richard Powell Unsettles Race and Color Theory
items.summary:
Sometime in the 1980s, when I was still a fledgling curator of 20th-century art at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, I was invited to the studio of a rather prominent artist. During our conversation, the work of Jacob Lawrence came up somehow, and the artist mentioned that he was impressed by what he described as Lawrence’s use of “Black” colors. Did I mention this artist was White? 

I was gobsmacked by the comment. Not that I wasn’t attuned to stereotypical societal associations of color — most notably, of bright, loud colors with Black people. In the 1950s, a full three decades before Nancy Reagan practically made red her official color, my Aunt Ruth was appalled that my mother made red coats for my sister and me, rather than using more acceptable pastel colors. Then a friend who grew up in Northern Ireland told me that Protestant Irish factions associated Catholic Irish with loud and bright colors. 

But how did such racially associative ideas translate to the realm of the so-called “fine” arts? I was aware of the place of color theory in the practice of art and knew the names of important theorists, from Johann Wolfgang von Goethe to Johannes Itten to Josef Albers. But otherwise, I presumed artists’ palettes were the result of personal predilection, technical explorations (i.e., the opening up of brushstrokes and form in the 19th century and the introduction of a wall of color in the 20th century), or cultural orientation. So it was therefore with great interest that I approached reading Richard Powell’s latest publication, Colorstruck!: Painting, Pigment, Affect (2026).
items.t: Richard Powell Unsettles Race and Color Theory

items.title: Guadalupe Maravilla to Offer Midnight Mass Sound Bath at St. John the Divine Cathedral
items.summary:
As part of his forthcoming Creative Time commission at the Cathedral of St. John the Divine, artist Guadalupe Maravilla will offer a bevy of programming beginning December 18.

Titled Consejos de las Estrellas and presented in collaboration with the Clemente Soto Vélez Cultural and Educational Center, the project comprises a sculptural installation that will “serve as a healing instrument and a place to find warmth and belonging when the holidays deepen the feeling of absence,” as Maravilla told ARTnews when the project was announced in October.

Core to Maravilla’s sculptures is their ability to be activated for sound baths, and Consejos de las Estrellas will offer eight sound baths during its run. Two of them will be staged in tandem with two winter holidays: a Christmas Eve Midnight Mass sound bath, beginning at 11:59 p.m. on December 24, and New Year Cleansing sound bath on January 9. The latter event will be proceeded by an herbal cleansing workshop by Herban Cura, which describes itself as a “healing justice herbalism and ecology school,” per its website.

A cancer survivor himself, Maravilla has long held sound baths specifically for the cancer community and he will offer two at St. John the Divine that will bookend this part of the programming. The first of these, on December 18, will be specifically for cancer survivors, healthcare workers, and caregivers and realized in partnership with the Mount Sinai Tisch Cancer Center. The final one will be staged on February 4, which is also World Cancer Day.

items.t: Guadalupe Maravilla to Offer Midnight Mass Sound Bath at St. John the Divine Cathedral

items.title: Iconic and Independent: New York Studio School's MFA Program
items.summary:
What does it mean to give art the time and attention it requires? Since its founding in 1964, the New York Studio School (NYSS) has pursued this question through an approach to art education grounded in sustained studio practice, rigorous inquiry, and the conviction that artists develop through the ongoing process of making, looking, and thinking. 

Located at 8 West 8th Street in Greenwich Village, the School occupies a building with a rich history in American art. Founded by artist and educator Mercedes Matter, NYSS carries forward a tradition of independent thinking and experimentation, offering an environment where artists can challenge assumptions, investigate fundamental questions, and develop their work through direct engagement with materials and ideas. 

Qinqin Li (MFA 2027) drawing in South Green Studio  The School’s full-time, two-year Master of Fine Arts (MFA) program is a 60-credit degree centered on intensive, individual studio practice in drawing, painting, sculpture, and art history. Rather than prescribing a single artistic direction, the program provides students with the time, space, and mentorship to pursue their own questions and cultivate their own distinctive artistic language. 

At the heart of the New York Studio School MFA program is the relationship between individual practice and collective exchange. Students are assigned private or semi-private studio spaces and select two core faculty artists to serve as their atelier mentors. Through studio visits, group critiques, and ongoing dialogue with faculty and peers, students are encouraged to…
items.t: Iconic and Independent: New York Studio School's MFA Program

items.title: Art World Advice Columnists Chen & Lampert Answered Questions as Old as Time
items.summary:
The disquieting question of how to be human in the art world came in for special consideration during a talk with advice columnists Chen & Lampert during Art Week NYC , a citywide festival organized by ARTnews , Artforum , and Art in America .

Together, Howie Chen and Andrew Lampert talked about their individual and collective efforts as artists, curators, and incomparable visionaries whose recurring “Hard Truths” advice columns and accompanying “Hard Choices” interactive quizzes are highlights of every issue of Art of America . Since their debut in 2019, the two writers have mulled pressing questions—can senior citizens be sage social-media ambassadors for museums in need of street cred? should a jilted artist keep applying for grants? is our advice helpful?—while dishing out wisdom for the ages.

At their talk on Friday, November 13 at the PMC Studio in Midtown Manhattan, Chen & Lampert reminisced about fielding queries from the past as well as their trip to Las Vegas for a 2025 essay titled “ Art and Ecstatic Ambience in Las Vegas’s Neon Vortex .” (A little taste of that, for old time’s sake: “Some writers go on Hajj to Marfa to feel the minimalist wind blow sand into their eyes, while others schlep Brooklinen tote bags as they chase biennials across small European cities. Being earnest art-world advice columnists, we prefer to explore more democratic forms of visual culture—the kind that ribaldly stages a two-hour revue called The Empire Strips Back: A Burlesque Parody .”)

items.title: James McAvoy’s random encounter triggers a delusional fantasy in Parasocial Activity
items.summary:
Òran Mór, Glasgow
In Briony Martha’s compelling play, a woman generates an alternative ending to her impromptu meeting with the Scottish superstar

Knowing what to believe is getting harder. Technology has blurred the line between truth and lies. Certain facts, though, we can demonstrate. We know, for example, that James McAvoy appeared in Cyrano de Bergerac at the Theatre Royal in Glasgow in the mask-wearing spring of 2022. We can also take playwright Briony Martha at her word when she says she bumped into the actor in a nearby coffee shop.

It is even true that McAvoy was in the audience of Martha’s Parasocial Activity towards the end of this summer’s run on the Edinburgh fringe: a performance that can only have had a heightened air of unreality.

items.title: Laura Hoptman Wins CCS Bard’s 2027 Audrey Irmas Award for Curatorial Excellence
items.summary:
The Center for Curatorial Studies at Bard College (CCS Bard) has given its 2027 Audrey Irmas Award for Curatorial Excellence to Laura Hoptman, executive director of New York’s Drawing Center. She will receive $25,000 and will be honored at CCS Bard’s spring gala in April.

Hoptman joined the Drawing Center in 2018 following eight years as a curator in the department of painting and sculpture at the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA). While at MoMA, she oversaw major traveling exhibitions devoted to Isa Genzken (2013) and Bruce Conner (2016), as well as the museum’s hotly debated survey of contemporary painting, “The Forever Now” (2014–2015).

After beginning her career as an assistant curator at the Bronx Museum, Hoptman worked as an assistant curator in MoMA’s department of drawings from 1996 to 2002. In 2003 she guest-curated “Drawing Now: Eight Propositions,” featuring more than 200 representational works by 26 contemporary artists, at MoMA QNS, and in 2004 she was director of the 54th Carnegie International in Pittsburgh. Between 2006 and 2010 she was senior curator at the New Museum in New York, where she co-organized “Unmonumental: The Object in the 21st Century” (2007–2008) and “The Generational: Younger than Jesus” (2009).

The Audrey Irmas Award has been given annually since 1998 and recognizes “groundbreaking visionaries in the curatorial field,” according to a press release. Past recipients include Adriano Pedrosa, Connie Butler, Carolyn Christov-Bakargiev, Thelma Golden, and Okwui Enwezor.

“Laura’s longstanding curatorial practice has furthered new art historical…

items.title: Recovering Edward Said’s Voice
items.summary:
For decades, the word “Palestinian” conjured a very specific image in the minds of many intellectuals and members of the public: the commanding presence of Edward Said, credited with no less than revolutionizing our collective understanding of the dynamics of oppression. Now, as Israel’s genocide in Gaza continues, Said’s legacy is not just urgent, but also, in some spaces, the target of censorship . Today, author Moustafa Bayoumi, who studied under the late critic, activist, and professor at Columbia University, pens a thoughtful review of Edward Said: Between Worlds (2026), a new documentary by Maiken Baird whose audio consists almost entirely of Said’s own words. “To recover Said’s voice is to rediscover some of the most compelling arguments that have been made for Palestinian liberation,” Bayoumi writes.

Can contemporary art make us laugh (and not just when we’re making fun of it)? Greta Rainbow visits a New York exhibition that’s all about embracing humor in art, and somewhere between Brian Belott's absurdist fan-embedded assemblages and Ebecho Muslimova’s delightfully transgressive depictions, she learns a thing or two about her own funny bone.

His manner and actions often seeming like improbable caricature, the current US president sets a challenge for satire, any comic exaggeration likely to be trumped by reality. Mike Bartlett’s play The 47th (2022), staged between Trump’s administrations, pursued wild fantasies about the politician’s future career that were soon superseded by odder events. Closer to Abbasi’s approach, Donald by the Italian dramatist Stefano Massini resembles his play The Lehman Trilogy – an international hit about the banking dynasty – in being a psychological analysis played by three actors with lightning switches of character and costume. Sheen is in wondrous voice as Owain Glyndŵr, clashing with Henry IV, in Gary Owen’s stirring history play for Welsh National Theatre

No one does rousing like Michael Sheen. Whether urging on the Welsh World Cup squad or vowing “apocalypse” on The Traitors, he surges forward on waves of rhetoric. As Owain Glyndŵr, beacon of Welsh resistance, he doesn’t disappoint. “We can die gently and be forgotten,” he exhorts his followers. “Or we can rage.”

Rage and resignation, the sword and the song, resonate through Gary Owen’s absorbing medieval epic for Wales Millennium Centre and Sheen’s new Welsh National Theatre. Glyndŵr is a marginal figure in Shakespeare’s Henry IV plays, a thorn in the unstable king’s side. Here he stands central, a fitting protagonist for a moment of both surging populist politics and a disillusionment with power play.

items.title: Is My Art Funny to You?
items.summary:
Ebecho Muslimova, “Fatebe Blow and Float” (2024) (image courtesy the artist and Magenta Plains, New York) Genuine laughter — involuntary, unplanned — is rare. Called “Duchenne laughter” after a 19th-century neurologist, the gesture is bodily, sometimes to a repulsive degree. But most of the time, we laugh because we feel that we should — that it would behoove us socially. In a talk at the Aspen AIR Festival this year, poet and psychoanalyst Nuar Alsadir described eliciting Duchenne laughter as an attempt “to strip away the layers of socialization and the false self.” While laughter “flies under the radar because of our associations to it as being joyful,” when you dig deeper, it’s “usually coming from some kind of conflict in the unconscious.”

What to make of art that makes us laugh? (Or at least desperately wants to?) Does This Taste Funny?: Humor in Contemporary Art , a sprawling exhibition across at Lehman College Art Gallery in the Bronx and The Gallery at Heimbold Visual Arts Center at Sarah Lawrence in Bronxville, proposes comedy as a potent artistic device. Co-curators Melissa Brown , artist and professor of art at Lehman College, and John O’Connor, artist and chair of the Visual and Studio Arts program at Sarah Lawrence, use humor’s various tones — absurd, cringe, slapstick, ironic — as organizing principles to present the work of 41 artists. From museum-collection heavy hitters like Ray Johnson and Cindy Sherman, to established cartoonists Roz Chast and Aline Kominsky-Crumb, to contemporary rising stars such as Ebecho Muslimova, Does This Taste Funny? implores us…
items.t: Is My Art Funny to You?

items.title: A Marquee Week of Indulgence
items.summary:
My mom called me greedy in jest this weekend because I had the gall to eat … more than five (but fewer than 10!) square slices of a delicious ube cake in her presence. Unlike each savored bite of that addictive purple pastry, I took her criticism on the chin because I believe that greed and indulgence function as a Venn diagram rather than as synonyms. And because there was still plenty of cake to go around.

Indulgence is in the air right now, and not just because we’re closing in on Thanksgiving weekend. Marquee auctions have rolled in like a thick fog on Monday, not long after the ADAA fair and an adjunctive torrential downpour rinsed the last of art fair season out of New York late last week. A press release from Sotheby’s informed me that $1.1 billion worth of art will go under the hammer this month, underpinned by today’s sale of a rarely seen van Gogh landscape expected to fetch a record-breaking $180 million. A brief shakeup ensued less than a week before the painting goes to auction, as the descendants of its former owner suddenly called on Sotheby’s to withdraw the work , alleging that it was sold under duress due to Nazi persecution. 

Don’t worry, though — the auction house shared in a follow-up release that the descendants and the Blaquier-Arrieta family, who are selling the painting alongside 11 other multimillion-dollar masterpieces from their collection, have come to a “mutually satisfactory resolution” that allows the sale to proceed as scheduled.

Really glad they worked that out. 

On the other side of the same coin, protesters gathered outside of the…
items.t: A Marquee Week of Indulgence

items.title: Arpita Singh, Indian Painter Who Never Stopped Innovating, Dies at 89
items.summary:
In Memoriam honors those we recently lost in the art world. 

Arpita Singh (1937–2026)
 Indian painter who bridged fantasy and reality 

One of the most high-profile contemporary Indian artists, Singh fused violent realism and fantasy imagery, constantly innovating across a six-decade career. In the 1970s and '80s, for instance, she explored abstraction, producing spare compositions filled with dots and dashes. She became more widely known in the West due to an exhibition at Serpentine Galleries just last year. 

"Singh never settles into a mode or style," critic John Yau wrote in a 2017 review of her exhibition at New Delhi- and New York-based Talwar Gallery for this magazine. "This body of work, which is being shown for the first time in America, is a singular achievement."

items.title: MoMA to Host First US Ana Mendieta Retrospective in Over 20 Years
items.summary:
The indelible impact of late Cuban-American artist Ana Mendieta 's practice will be celebrated in a forthcoming retrospective in New York next year. Scheduled to open at the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) in Manhattan in December 2027, Ana Mendieta: A Retrospective marks the first presentation of Mendieta's overarching career in the United States in over 20 years. 

MoMA's announcement comes just two months before Tate Modern's ongoing Mendieta retrospective closes in London. Comprising around 200 works, including rarely seen formative drawings and newly remastered films, the MoMA exhibition will present Mendieta's artistic process, signature developments, and career milestones in a chronological fashion. Starting with early figurative works completed during her undergraduate and graduate studies at the University of Iowa, the exhibition will follow the artist's subsequent expansion in making and documenting her performance art, as well as her foray into sculpture, installation, and site-specific land art.

Born in Cuba and raised in Iowa from age 12 as a child evacuee through Operation Peter Pan, Mendieta ruminated on themes of displacement, ancestral memory, ecology, and the politics of the female body, as well as its connection with the natural world. She's best known for her Silueta (1973–80) series, in which the outline of her body (either present or absent) is embedded, extruded, burned, or embellished into various natural environments as a physical and spiritual reunion with the earth. These “earth-body works,” as Mendieta called them, dealt with Mesoamerican and…
items.t: MoMA to Host First US Ana Mendieta Retrospective in Over 20 Years

items.title: Edward Said Speaks More Urgently Than Ever
items.summary:
In their (still brilliant) 1990 experimental film Introduction to the End of an Argument , filmmakers Jayce Salloum and Elia Suleiman splice together troves of found footage about Palestinians and Israelis. The result is an exquisite mash-up of Hollywood cartoons and political clichés, a comic pastiche illustrating the common bond between Orientalism and zombies. Both just won’t die.  

While Salloum and Suleiman’s film consists mostly of news clips and film reels, one of Gaza’s elder statesmen, the late Haider Abdul Shafi, does appear briefly twice. In one scene, Abdul Shafi, sitting at a nondescript table, is asked by an interviewer: “Is it your belief that if a Palestinian state was created, there would be lasting peace in the Middle East?” Just as he’s about to respond, the film mischievously cuts away, in an edit loaded with meaning. Palestinians may be seen in Western media, the film is telling us, but they cannot be heard from.

Maiken Baird’s new documentary, Edward Said: Between Worlds (2026), joyfully demonstrates how Edward Said was the exception to this semi-official ban on Palestinians representing themselves. Like Salloum and Suleiman, Baird also sifts through reservoirs of found footage, though the result couldn’t be more different. Offering a rough chronology of Said’s life, Baird’s film celebrates him by highlighting his contributions and lasting influence in numerous domains, from literary theory to American foreign policy. 

For decades, the Columbia University professor of comparative literature was the most famous, if not the only, Palestinian…
items.t: Edward Said Speaks More Urgently Than Ever

items.title: Kelly Gough is simply astounding as Desire Under the Elms reaches the heights of Greek tragedy
items.summary:
Almeida theatre, London
Part-Phaedra and part-Medea, Gough is mesmerising in Ebenezer Bamgboye’s stylised staging of Eugene O’Neill’s family drama

You would not know that Eugene O’Neill’s play was originally set on a mid 19th-century farm. This version by director Ebenezer Bamgboye brings modernity with its sleek storytelling, but also nods to the ancient Greek drama O’Neill was emulating in his 1924 play about illicit desire and the father-son fight for land.

It makes for a strange mix at first, beguiling and bewildering in equal measure. Bamgboye employs some of the striking theatricality that he brought to his magnetic adaptation of The Lonely Londoners two years ago. It is an original refashioning, the script sharper with less of the exposition that might date it, but the directorial flourishes come so thick and fast that it is stylised to the bone. Bamgboye has previously worked with Rebecca Frecknall (who staged the leaden O’Neill drama A Moon for the Misbegotten last year) and the first half seems to pay too big a debt to her style of work.

items.summary:
Before an assassination attempt on Andy Warhol in 1968, Solanas used her fierce writing to confront male supremacy. What can her work teach us about expressing raw anger?

It is exhausting to always express anger constructively and reasonably – especially when what you are angry about is violence, exploitation and the inexcusable appetite of disgusting, powerful, greedy men to gain yet more power.

Could you please be more balanced in how you express yourself? Could you make your objection to the destruction of the world – through violating not only women but also the planet – well, more constructive? Could you be a little less unpleasant in your anger?

items.summary:
A radical new take on the modernist classic includes a Berlin ketamine binge, a ‘goon cave’ and an all-trans cast. The manifesto? To ‘desecrate’ expectations

As Orlando’s on a comedown after a ket-heavy night out in Berlin, surrounded by a group of sharp-tongued trans sex workers, Charli Cowgill and Laurie Ward pause the read-through. The scene is new and “it’s feeling a little safe,” Ward says, drumming the table. “How can we make it riskier?”

Cowgill and Ward are piss/CARNATION, a theatre-making duo creating fearless, messy and intellectually rigorous work. Audience spit was collected and thrown in their first production, 52 Monologues for Young Transsexuals, a show that collated trans women’s experiences of men and sex work. Ugly Sisters, the pair’s riotous follow-up, relived a brief encounter between a trans woman and Germaine Greer who wrote a caustic article about it. “As a company,” Ward says, “we tend more towards brutal than twee.”

The Three Lives of Lucie Cabrol by Complicité conjured the struggles of a French village with an intense rawness

There are many things you see that are impactful, but few you can genuinely say change your life. I saw Complicité’s The Three Lives of Lucie Cabrol aged 16 on a school trip to Riverside Studios in London and it really reached me. I’d been educated in a very language, words-based way. Here the story was told – with such intensity! – through people’s bodies.

The world they were conjuring, from a story by John Berger in his book Pig Earth, was about this remote French village – a world of labour. And the strife and struggles of these characters was expressed through the physical work of the company.

Exclusive: Trailer released for Rambert’s version of Russell T Davies’s show about friendship amid the 80s Aids crisis and the ‘extraordinary freedom’ of clubbing

Russell T Davies’s award-winning series It’s a Sin, about young gay friends living through the Aids crisis in 1980s London, is getting a new life as a dance piece, with a trailer released on Monday ahead of an opening at Aviva Studios in Manchester in February.

“We had a few approaches, but a lot of people wanted to make it a musical, which made my heart sink slightly,” said Davies. “I always imagined an aria between those two women on the seafront at the end and I thought: ‘Oh, that could be so terrible!’” Dance was different, he said. “It felt so original and so pure. The story distils down to these emotional moments that are going to be done so beautifully on stage.”

items.title: Tamsin Greig is sensational in a Cranford where comedy and pain are in perfect balance
items.summary:
Orange Tree theatre, London
This streamlined adaptation of Elizabeth Gaskell’s novel gets right to the heart of her characters, who face heartbreak and loss but gain from the strength of female friendship

There’s more than one worry for any new dramatisation of Elizabeth Gaskell’s novel to contend with. There is the risk of this story, set among the unmarried women and widows of a fictional English town, being considered Middlemarch lite – and overshadowed by the Royal Shakespeare Company’s luminous adaptation of the George Eliot novel, currently running in Stratford-Upon-Avon. Then there is the 2007 BBC adaptation of Cranford, which threw every national treasure at it, trowelling on the lovable humour and sentiment as it did so.

This production, however, co-created by Lin Coghlan, Shaun McKenna and Josh Roche, bypasses all those dangers by leaning into theatricality – and sheer good acting. The script is by Coghlan and McKenna, who previously adapted The Forsyte Saga, staged last year by the RSC. They confidently fillet the original and also add their own little inventions.

Continue reading...
